On Oct 17, 3:15 am, tony.a...@gmail.com wrote:
> What about Combat as a viable path to victory? Why are the only
> effective cards so far to support that strategy been Fame, Tension,
> and Dragon Bound?

I often hear people ask some variant of this question, "Why
doesn't combat win games?" But I think this reflects a wrong way of
looking at the game. I agree that an all-combat deck doesn't win, but
neither does an all-stealth deck. Do you put 60 stealth cards in a
deck and say, "My stealth deck sucks, why doesn't stealth win games?"
Of course not. Stealth is great, as part of a larger strategy
involving good actions to use the stealth on--and combat is the same.

I would like to see better combat cards in the future (on the
level of Torn Signpost or Theft of Vitae) because that's how good
combat cards have to be to reach competitive play. (I specifically
hope Quietus can get some good long-range strikes.) But I would not
say that combat is or ever should be a way to win games on its own,
any more than stealth is, or should be.

Tremere, Brujah, Tzimisce, Ahrimanes, and !Nosferatu all can make
finals tables with loads of combat cards in their decks, sometimes
more than 30. I think that shows combat has an important role in the
game. But they don't win BY fighting--any more than Malkavians win BY
stealthing.

If someday there are enough cards to encourage players to make
proactive, Bum's Rush-based decks which oust their prey for doing
that, then I think a lot of players will start to really hate playing
against combat. It will force a lot of players to include 20+ combat
defense cards just in order to be allowed to remain ready. That
increases the likelihood that a player will not be able to play his/
her game, and also I think increases the rock/paper/scissors crapshoot
element of V:TES. I'm opposed to all this.

In conclusion, I think combat is an important part of the game
which will continue to shine in some decks, but which should not be
transformed into a victory condition.

-- Brian

that effectively removes your minions from the ready region takes away

interesting trick decks and so on) will just slowly die. And so will

that day will come sooner that we think if the combat develops at the

powerful. Still. Old school/new school S+B decks still win all the
time. 'Cause they are amazingly effective. What kills them more than
anything else? Rush combat. But for Rush combat to make a show on the
scene, Rush combat needs to be a viable way to win.

Rush combat was, until recently, a just barely viable way to win games/
tournaments. It was a hard path to follow, sure, but doable. The
Imbued knocked the viability of Rush combat back some in a grand
sense, which was sad, but maybe something that will get fixed.

> If someday there are enough cards to encourage players to make

There already are enough cards to encourage players to make proactive,
Bum's Rush based decks which oust their prey for doing that. See:
Fame, Tension, Dragonbound, Perpetual Care (all of which are notably
useless against the Imbued...). Rush decks can and do work. They are
just a little below the "generally effective" line these days.

A lot of people complain the Rush combat isn't "fun", as it keeps
folks from playing the game. As noted, lots of decks do that all the
time. Getting bled for 20 in 4 turns? Keeps you from playing the game.
Having your vampires burned by PTO? Keeps you from playing the game.
Having all your minions Brainwashed? Keeps you from playing the game.
Getting all your dudes Sensory Deprived? Keeps you from playing the
game.

VTES can be a mean game. A lot of the time, if your predator is
effective? You don't get to play. That is sad. But how it goes. Heck--
in our LotN draft tournament recently, I got ousted by a more or less
preconstructed Giovanni deck in, like, 12 minutes from start time. I
spent the next hour and a half being like "Huh. That was fairly brutal
for a pre-con. Man." and not having anything to do but watch other
games. Which was fine, as that is sometimes what happens.

> It will force a lot of players to include 20+ combat
> defense cards just in order to be allowed to remain ready.

You mean like how currently, players are forced to include 20+ bleed
defense cards just in order to be allowed to remain in the game?

Defense is a choice. Currently, bleed defense is usually the top
choice, 'cause bleed is a default action, and the likelyhood of being
powerbled is high enough for the opprtunity cost of including specific
bleed defense (how many deck include, at the very least 6-8 wake type
card/8-10 bounce? Most of them...)

People don't generally consider combat to be a winning strategy, so
they don't expect to see it much, so they don't include much combat
defense. Which is a reasonable thing to do. But then they get cranky
when they get rushed and killed. Much like sometimes people get cranky
when they get powerbled to death when they included zero bleed defense
in their deck. That is just how things go.

> That
> increases the likelihood that a player will not be able to play his/
> her game, and also I think increases the rock/paper/scissors crapshoot
> element of V:TES. I'm opposed to all this.

The RPS crapshoot is already a huge element of the game. Except that
people regularly throw Scisors (i.e. bleeding), so including Scisor
defense is just common wisdom. Rush decks do ok 'cause they throw
Rock.

> In conclusion, I think combat is an important part of the game
> which will continue to shine in some decks, but which should not be
> transformed into a victory condition.

It already is a victory condition. Just a more protracted one than
bleeding for 6 per action.

-Peter

Agreed, and it was my initial reaction at the first post.

I've played recently at the french Championship, after nearly a year without
playing (not even regular casual play, truly) and I've had to face the
following facts :

- many fight decks scored GWs and made the finals
- among them were all the variations : allies rush, weenie rush (Ani
mostly), intercept fight (Trems, Tzim, Ani, Aus/guns), bruise'n'vote,
bruise'n'bleed, Eurobrujah toolbox crap (sick of them after so many years),
etc.
- there were so many fighters that to survive you had to either pack combat
love or lots of combat hate
- of course weenies were better able to handle the rushers than fatties (2
weenies dead = you get out another weenie ; 2 Inner Circles dead, as I
witnesses, = well, you're dead you know ?!)
- as a result of all this, decks which I built according to the game I used
to play 1 year ago - and with which I made big scores in big tournies - were
close to useless, and I got my ass handed to me on a silver plate (granted,
I played less well than a year ago too, but the decks did have something to
do with it too)

So my conclusion is : there definitely has been a change in metagame towards
fight, mainly intercept/fight and rush/fight, either as part or total of a
winning strategy (the rest might include bleed or vote, always good to, you
know, kill a prey or two...).

This already requires adapting to, as I can testify. More than this and we
might as well play Rage all over and forget all about politics, not to
mention bleed. Oh, and playing big vampires - with the possible exception of
Enkidu - has definitely become too risky to be worth mentionning at a normal
tournament.

with.

in the end, the Imbued being viable and regularly showing up in
tournaments means that Rush combat is often fighting a much bigger
uphill battle than it can deal with.

Sure. 11 years ago.

Taste, when originally printed, existed in an environment where allies
were a minor sideline, at best. Yeah, that Taste didn't work on allies
had some extra background flavor to it, which was a plus I'm sure, but
in a game design sense, there wasn't any need for Taste to work on
Allies. As they didn't show up much and didn't have much life in the
first place to Taste. Making Taste not work on allies was totally
reasonable, when Taste was printed. And then reprinted. Until the
Imbued came out.

Fame, when printed, was a totally different card. And keyed off of
"going to torpor". Allies didn't go to torpor, or anything similar, so
as Fame had an effect that happened from going to torpor and a
permanent effect that came from being in torpor, it made perfect sense
to make it only work on vampires. Especially as, again, allies were
almost a total non factor in the game when Fame was printed. And then
when Fame was totally reworked, allies still were virtially a zero
factor in the game.

So it made total sense, at the time, for Taste and Fame (and whatever)
to not work on allies. As they didn't need to.

Then the Imbued came out.

And I can understand that once the Imbued came out, there wasn't going
to be a massive re-write of all the cards that said "vampire" instead
of "minion", 'cause there are an awful lot of them. But this strikes
me as a different path than "Taste was specifically designed to not
work on the Imbued".

Sure, one could say that the Imbued were specifically designed to not
be Tasted (or Famed or Havened or Disarmed or Seductioned or
whatever), but that turned out to be, IMHO, something that isn't
working out so well.

-Peter

The trouble with this suggestion - as opposed to simply changing the
existing cards through errata or reprinting - is that it effectively
reduces the value of combat in the metagame anyway. It may reduce
it less than is currently the case (that is, in comparison with the
reduction of its matrix game value caused by Imbued decks appearing
on the scene) but I don't think the change makes much difference.

Bear with me here for a moment. When you add a new card to the game
that's intended to be the equivalent of card X but has a slightly
different set of costs and effects, that can be a good thing as is
the case of adding Forced Awakening to a card mix that already has
Wake with Evenings Freshness. This allows more intercept-and-combat-
oriented and less bounce-oriented decks a better option for the same
effect and allows people to vary their approach to reaction untap
cards, leading in turn to more interesting deckbuilding problems.
But - notice - it _deliberately_ doesn't change the value of reaction
untap very much. It increases it slightly for certain types of decks
that are more amendable to the one use (intercept) than the other
(bounce). But the change is intentionally small.

In the case of, for instance, your altered Fame, your stated intent
is likewise not to change the value of Fame. (I'm assuming one
couldn't play both the new card AND Fame on a vampire. This, in
itself, would make a huge difference in its value since using the
two together would be pretty strong.) It's to give players an
interesting choice which hinges on whether they expect to prey on
almost all vampire decks or a more mixed set of prey which includes
more Imbued decks. But giving players an interesting choice doesn't
solve your original problem. What I think you really want, Peter,
is to directly increase the value of combat decks against Imbued
decks. This requires that cards typically used by combat decks be
just as good as they currently are against vampire decks while
becoming _simultaneously_ better against Imbued decks. Thus, the
combat deck can't be required to swap out Fame. It needs to be
allowed to use Fame against the Imbued.

It may be that Fame needn't make the Famed Imbued's controller lose
three pool. The new Fame might still cost three when the minion
it were played on was a vampire but only two when played on an
Imbued. But I think you have to do something like that to change
the game in the way (I believe) you're looking to change it.

Fred

combat in it can win games, but that's not the combat winning.

something like 8 Deflection and 8 Majesty. Against a bleeder, paired
with his general defense, he'll probably do fine. Against a rush
deck? I doubt his majesties are going to matter. Arika is dead, and
nothing short of that rush deck having a super-dangerous predator is
going to stop that.

same, as they are playable (and often quite good) when you have a
predator who doesn't bleed you at all.

much in the way of "general defense" which also works very well
against combat.

bleed me) and Majesty (you didn't just fight me): There is no card

would have needed to survive.

> Rock.

People often choose to play with 6-10 cards that only work against
getting bled, and 6-10 cards that only work against getting beat up.
Making cards that make it realistic that combat decks can oust you
_with the combat itself_, without bleeding or voting, would probably
increase the number of combat decks in each tournament, and
necessarily the combat defense per deck. Similarly, making action
modifiers that cancel bounce cards or prevent them from being played
would probably increase the "mandatory" bleed defense per deck.

But again, it's a poor comparison. Combat's harder to defend against
than bleeding, bleeding's more direct than combat. A better
comparison is combat and stealth, I think. Undead Strength being
comparable to Lost in Crowds in this way, Psyche! to Elder
Impersonation, or Majesty to Draba.

> > which will continue to shine in some decks, but which should not be
> > transformed into a victory condition.
>
> It already is a victory condition. Just a more protracted one than
> bleeding for 6 per action.

Just because a deck wins and happens to have combat in it, does not
make combat a victory condition. The guy who started the first post
wanted more cards which made "I beat your guy up" mean you lose pool,
too. If that sort of thing gets printed enough such that it's
seriously as viable as stealth bleed, then the whole game will be
totally different from how it is now. Most current decks will not be
remotely viable. Every player will need gobs of combat cards just to
survive.

Exciting variant, but I wouldn't want to play it every couple of
weeks. 8 Deflection, 8 Majesty is a perfectly reasonable amount of
"mandatory" defense in my book, and we can all leave the other 74 card
slots to providing for general defense, setting ourselves up, and
generating offense of our own.

-- Brian

combat cards in my deck as it's pointless.

And getting back to the original poster's concern: Yes, I would be
upset if there were some card which allowed that deck to win just for
RPS'ing the whole metagame that way.

> > And I think that's really a lot of bounce, most decks using 6-8
> > Deflections. Wakes are multi-purpose, so is intercept and Blood
> > Dolls; the only bleed-specific defenses are seven of the bounce cards.
>
> Well by your own choices you went more with Deflect than TM. And
> there are clearly more powerful (or at least a variety of) other
> intercept cards, yet you only used TM. So clearly for the bounce. I
> think this line of defense is a bit disingenuous.

What? Why would you think that I didn't use any other intercept
cards? Just to make things clear for the rest of this, here are the
general defenses that deck had (not the whole decklist):

Intercept and wakes:
2 Carna, The Princess Witch
1 KRCG News Radio
1 Aranthebes, the Immortal
8 Forced Awakening
1 Mr. Winthrop
1 Sport Bike
6 Enhanced Senses
3 Telepathic Misdirection
2 Magic of the Smith (if I need Sport Bike)

Blood/pool gain:
1 Academic Hunting Ground
1 Arcane Library
3 Blood Doll
2 Dreams of the Sphinx
1 Giant's Blood
1 Powerbase: Montreal
1 Rack, The
1 University Hunting Ground
13 Govern the Unaligned
10 Theft of Vitae

And of course, the deck also defended itself with 6 Deflection and 1
Redirection.

That totals to 66 cards in a 90 card deck all usable for intercept,
untap, or blood gain, and only 7 of them are restricted to "only being
usable against bleeds". This is really a small portion of the deck,
enough that it didn't jam me up.

> > Why does rush combat have to be a whole strategy, any more than
> > Corruption counters has to be? Why can't combat just be a big part of
> > many larger strategies?
>

> There's just a lot of evidence, including statements from various
> designers, that this just isn't so. Combat, vote, and bleed were
> envisioned as a triangle. Apparently it was intentional with cards
> like Bum's Rush that you could rush your prey's guys, "force" him to
> spend more on new guys, rush those, and then finish the job with your
> paltry bleeds of one (or whatever). That isn't the only way to use
> red cards, but from what I understand it was really and truly intended
> as a major path to victory. Unlike Corruption, or whatever other
> secondary-resource-attacking thing you want to substitute.

OK, I accept that argument. I'm not sure that that means we should
continue pursuing that dream until it is realized regardless of the
cost to the game's diversity, though.

> > > > If someday there are enough cards to encourage players to make
> > > > proactive, Bum's Rush-based decks which oust their prey for doing
> > > > that, then I think a lot of players will start to really hate playing
> > > > against combat.
>
> Maybe they will balance out with all the people who have attempted to
> do that which we've been led to believe should be doable, and now
> suddenly is. Conservation of satisfaction?

Nah, one of the things that makes V:TES a good game is that players
interact via card play quite a bit. If combat gets good enough to
where you need 30-40 combat cards in order to survive until your first
action, I really doubt it'll be very interactive at all.

See, bleeding defaults to your prey, so that you can't just pool your
resources with another player to bleed a guy out directly. But Bum's
Rush doesn't have that default. And if you think two combat decks
sitting next to each other is a bad thing, cause they'll both lose the
game, then imagine three sitting in a row. Or all five players
playing combat, and the one who has the trumpiest combat wins, or
worse, the one who gets in the most combats loses. Sorry, not
interested. Combat functions well right now, and just needs some more
powerful cards. It does NOT need to be transformed into a victory
condition.

> And again, speaking as someone who brings a lot of combat: a moderate
> amount of combat defense goes a long way.

I've played against your Fatima multirush deck a couple times, and
it's only a lot of combat _compared to what you would expect to see_.
It is not very much combat at all, compared to some of the crap I've
been expected to hang on through.

And I'll "sort-of" concede a point right now: If rush combat IS
given, let's say, a non-unique Fame or something, and it can oust
players, and the BEST WAY TO DO THAT just so happens to be in a way
where a moderate amount of combat defense can handle it, then I'm not
opposed. I'm not in favor, mind you, but I don't think it would hurt
the game all that much.

But why would players rush with 40 combat cards, when they could rush
with 70? I mean, if it can oust your prey now, that is?

> Rush combat (and to a
> lesser extent intercept combat) are such piss-poor means of ousting
> people that even getting stymied a little bit can push you across the
> razor's edge from winning to losing.
>
> Combat is interesting, it's varied, it's a little game within a game.
> It's "fun". So you have to have 10 less stealth bleed cards and 10
> more red cards in the average deck, and actually play the combat
> game. That is so bad? That would make you like this game less? I
> guess it's just a subjective thing, but I don't get it.

Again, I don't think it would make players put in 10 more combat
defense cards. I think it would make some players include more combat
defense cards, until the point where the deck can't support itself
anymore, at which point they'll just say, "screw it, if I sit next to
rush combat, I'm dead anyway" and just play with no combat cards
instead. And then the game is less interactive, instead of more.

> > Good thing most of those don't hit the tournament scene with much
> > regularity. Bleeding hard sees play, and PTO, but then PTO doesn't
> > usually get called every turn such that you can't play at all.
>
> No, you can usually play about the first third of the game, the build-
> up part, until they cycle into their PTO(s). After that, if you dared
> to play a big guy, you are probably through playing. See any one of
> the ad nauseum PTO threads for more.

Yeah, but once again, where the hell are your Confusion of the Eye or
Delaying Tactics? DI is only general defense, but I think the other
two belong in most decks.

My point here is, you can react to the vote (which is one card) with
another one card, and that's fine. You can't do that with combat,
unless you know you're older than them and have Dominate, but I think
that's really limited use. I certainly won't claim that most decks
which fear rush would benefit from Obedience, since they're not all
large caps with dominate.

> > But they're not. Unless you count all wakes, intercept, pool gain,
> > and multipurpose defense cards (like Confusion of the Eye) as being
> > "bleed defense cards". I say these general defense cards aren't the
> > same, as they are playable (and often quite good) when you have a
> > predator who doesn't bleed you at all.
>
> I would say the wakes are mostly there to support the bounce. Not
> always, but I think it's fair to say it's common.

I think in large-cap decks, sure, it's common. It's also a problem, I
think, that so many decks choose to ignore reactions altogether, or
all reactions except wakes and bounce. Decks should be able to attack
AND defend, for an ideal game. But we're far from ideal, yet.

Anyway, in my decks anyway, Wakes aren't usually just for bounce.
When they are, it's usually something like 2 WWEF and 8 Deflection, so
hardly important.

> > But there's one huge difference between Deflection (you didn't just
> > bleed me) and Majesty (you didn't just fight me): There is no card
> > which does for anti-bleed-defense what Immortal Grapple or Psyche!
> > does for anti-combat-defense.
>
> Right. Because, as you admit, bleed directly attacks the primary
> resource and combat doesn't. Bleed needs to have a stronger trump
> than combat. I think you just don't like having to be involved in
> combat.

Hmm...I may be speaking too soon, but I believe that out of the last 6
years of continental championships here and in Europe, my deck used
the most combat cards (27) out of any of the winners. That's not a
guy who doesn't like being involved in combat--that's a guy who
recognizes combat's strength as part of a larger strategy.

> Lots of players feel that way. I don't feel like being
> involved in the bleed/intercept/bounce game. When are people going to
> start accommodating me?

I'm not asking to be accommodated in some ridiculously un-V:TES-like
way. I'm saying that the fun of combat, indeed the fun of the game,
is in NOT knowing who's going to win this combat, or who's going to
win this game, and having to interact through card play in order to
determine it. Currently, building a deck with 70 combat cards is
foolish, and punishes another player or two at random for sitting
there, and isn't a mystery who's going to win the combat, and is
itself punished by getting 0 vps. If this changes, and building a
deck with 70 combat cards is viable, then I don't think there will be
more interaction, but less. And, to tie this back into the beginning,
if the initial poster's wishes are granted (make rush combat a viable
means of ousting players), then I don't really see why decks with 70
combat cards wouldn't be viable, and therefore interaction would
probably decrease, and therefore the game would be less fun.

> > Ahh. See, I get cranky when I'm playing with 10 Majesty and 6 Rolling
> > with the Punches and I get rushed by a super-dedicated combat monster
> > and I only have 3 Majesties in my hand, which is 1 short of what I
> > would have needed to survive.
>
> I feel the same way about "super dedicated bleed/vote monsters." I
> would like the game more if people would accommodate me on that.

You can play with Deflections, or Delaying Tactics, or Confusions of
the Eye, as one-card solutions to your problems. But I cannot play
with one-card solutions that end a combat without my opponent already
having planned my defenses out of meaningful existence.

Combat is harder to stop because it doesn't win games by itself.

-- Brian

Messages.Author: Name.Luc...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
On Oct 19, 8:52 am, Peter D Bakija <p...@lightlink.com> wrote:
> On Oct 19, 5:01 am, Name.Luckynum...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> > No it doesn't. You may mean by extension that a deck with lots of
> > combat in it can win games, but that's not the combat winning.
>
> By that same logic, you can say that a deck with lots of bleed in it
> can win games, but it isn't the bleed cards that are winning.

No, I don't see how. I don't know whether you misinterpreted what I
was saying on purpose, but Bum's Rush culminates in exactly 0 pool
loss unless there's some other card in play which changes that. This
is unlike bleed cards, which increase the amount of pool to be lost
directly.

When Beast rushes you, and you have Fame, it's the Fame that's causing
you to lose pool, not Beast. This is an important distinction for
this conversation, because more Fame-like cards is what the OP seems
to be asking for.

> > Bleeding affects pool directly, and is a means of winning. Combat is
> > a way of getting bleeds to succeed, or reduce someone's secondary
> > resources, but does NOT oust on its own.
>
> Nothing ousts on its own by virtue of the semantic gymnastics you are
> applying here. Bleed cards do nothing on their own. You need minions
> to use them and take actions to bleed with them.

You and I both know you can't Bum's Rush someone to death. You can
Bum's Rush them out of minions, sure, but not to death. This
distinction matters with regard to the OP's request.

Also, I'm not engaging in "semantic gymnastics". I'm engaging in
"staying on topic". The OP said he wanted "combat [to be] a viable
path to victory", and cited Fame, Tension, and Dragonbound to be
examples of what he meant.

How do you interpret his question, if not the way I do?

Also, if OP is talking about rush decks that cannot realistically oust
by bleeding, and therefore need to be able to oust by rushing, then
why do you think your rush decks, which _can_ oust by bleeding, and do
not need to oust by rushing, are relevant in a conversation about
combat-as-victory-condition?

> > I bring out Lucretia, Cess Queen. Anybody scared yet? No? I
> > actually had a predator like this, at the EC this year, just Lucretia
> > Clan Impersonating Daughters and then Minion Tap/Concert
> > Tour...definitely a stealth bloat deck. Never going to oust me in a
> > million years, though, cause like I said, stealth doesn't win games.
>
> I bring out Arika. I go to bleed for 7. I'm blocked. My turn ends.
> Anybody scared yet? How is giving an example of a poorly built deck an
> example of anything?

A deck which just brings out Al-Ashrad and then rushes people is a
poorly built deck. Enter a new card which is basically a non-unique
Fame, and now it's not such a poorly built deck after all, is it?
That's the point: Just rushing and playing combat cards currently
doesn't win. With more fame-like cards, it could. But first I'm
making sure we're all on the same page with "just rushing and playing
combat cards currently doesn't win." It seems we're not on the same
page yet, cause you allow for a bruise and bleed style deck, which is
entirely unlike a pure-rush deck.

Do you agree that there could very reasonably exist a deck which
rushes very effectively, but bleeds poorly, and therefore doesn't oust
many preys, but which would be a very good deck if (say) Fame wasn't
unique?

Because if we agree that that deck probably exists, then we're close
enough to "on the same page" that I think we can move on to the next
part of the argument.

> > And it's important to recognize that a deck is hardly an all stealth
> > deck if it's bleeding forward with lots of small minions.
>
> You were trying to claim that stealth does not win games. Now you are
> trying to claim that stealth doesn't win games, as long as the stealth
> is used stupidly. Not really supporting your argument.

That was not my argument, but I'll pretend it was, in order to
demonstrate that my refutation of the OP stands even with a weak
version of my argument.

If we assume:
1. "Stealth doesn't win games, as long as the stealth is used
stupidly."
we can probably also assume:
2. "Combat doesn't win games, as long as the combat is used
stupidly."
and of course, introducing a card fulfilling OP's request:
3. "There should be cards that turn using combat stupidly into a
victory."
to see whether his request is sensible, consider:
4. "There should be cards that turn using stealth stupidly into a
victory."

Imagine a card that says that whenever your prey doesn't try to block
you, or tries and fails, he or she has to lose some amount of pool.
This would make an all-stealth strategy viable. But I'm still against
it, for the same reasons I'm against excessive printing of Fame-like
effects: Because stealth doesn't oust, because combat doesn't oust,
because they're part of the larger picture. These two are not ends
unto themselves, and I don't like cards that make them act as though
they are, because...

Well, you know how a deck with just stealth and bleed cards clumps
very little? Imagine it had JUST STEALTH CARDS. It would be
goddamned V:TES solitaire.

> There was no condition in your original assertion that "weenies" were
> not part of the equation. If your original assertion is "all stealth,
> when built into a bad deck, can't win games", then ok. But the issue
> there is "the bad deck" not "all stealth".

Which applies in the same way to combat. "All combat, when built into
a bad deck, can't win games." Example, just Beast and Theo Bell
trying to kill everything isn't particularly effective at getting GWs.

But, oh, look! It's non-unique Fame, or 20 different printed versions
of Fame, or whatever. Suddenly just rushing everything with Beast and
Theo IS particularly effective at getting GWs!

Don't you see a problem with this?

> > Regarding stealth-bleed being kept in check by rush combat: This
> > hasn't been my experience. I personally have found that bleed bounce
> > is the most effective "check" for s+b decks.
>

> Bounce slows S+B down. Killing all the S+B minions shuts S+B down.

Bounce turns the S+B deck into one of your tools for ousting your
prey. Killing all of ANYONE'S minions shuts them down, but doesn't
mean you win.

> > Why does rush combat have to be a whole strategy, any more than
> > Corruption counters has to be? Why can't combat just be a big part of
> > many larger strategies?
>

> It doesn't *have* to be. Nothing *has* to be. But it already is. And
> was significantly more effective pre-Imbued.

"Just" rush combat wasn't already effective. A deck which could bleed
a bunch of times and _also_ rush was a somewhat successful strategy,
as you've demonstrated, but that strategy doesn't need Fame for the
oust. And because of that, there's a big difference between your deck
(which worked fine) and what the OP was talking about (which is
apparently combat as a viable path to GWs in some deck which currently
DOESN'T win by just rushing people.)

> > Good thing most of those don't hit the tournament scene with much
> > regularity. Bleeding hard sees play, and PTO, but then PTO doesn't
> > usually get called every turn such that you can't play at all.

> > Besides, vote defense is becoming more prevalent, such that Delaying
> > Tactics and Confusion of the Eye are serious anti-vote measures you'll
> > see at practically every table.
>
> I'm unsure how this is relevant.

It was a list of things that stop you from being able to play.
However, the things listed are at best rare in serious play, and at
worst, non-existant. The remaining cards/deck types are something you
can defend against, and that's what I was trying to illustrate.

The relevance is, rush decks that preemptively rush all your guys stop
you from playing the game before you've started. This is not only
(IMHO) bad for the game, but the reason it's not a "supported"
strategy. Those strategies we listed which stop players from
interacting are given very little support, while those which encourage
interaction (stealth vs. intercept, vote vs. vote defense, etc.) are
given attention in almost every set.

> > But they're not. Unless you count all wakes, intercept, pool gain,
> > and multipurpose defense cards (like Confusion of the Eye) as being
> > "bleed defense cards".
>

> I'm counting wakes and bounce in decks that have no other reaction
> cards, at a bare minimum. Many, many decks include, as noted, 6-8 wake/
> 8-10 bounce. Simply to avoid getting powerbled to death.

OK, in a deck which is made only of offense, except it uses bounce,
and then wakes solely for the bounce, sure, wakes count as bleed
defense. I'll give you that.

However, in any deck which has both defense and offense, almost all of
your general defenses help you somewhat against powerbleed. Your
Blood Dolls and Minion Taps, your Dreams and Powerbase: Montreal, your
Govern or Enchant at superior, your intercept, wakes, you name it--all
of your "general" defenses still help you against bleeds. Which of
these will help you against combat? I've found wakes can stop the
maneuver from a Bum's Rush, but that's about it.

I interpreted the OP's request to be that rushing BY ITSELF should be
able to oust (with help from new Fame-like cards), which is currently
not the case. You happen to play a rush deck that bleeds for the
oust; he's talking about a deck which rushes for the oust. I _like_
your deck; I don't like his deck. His deck needs more "Fames" than
there currently are in order to win the game.

I hope I've explained my position well enough.

-- Brian

> I think that's odd that you'd say that people's choice to play more
> bounce doesn't deter players from bringing S&B. It certainly affects
> me. In fact, I try to notice when players are packing too many
> Deflections, or too many Delaying Tactics, or a whole fistful of extra

I must not be a good player then, since I don't do it, because I
really don't think it can be done. Just because I saw this or that
guy, or a few in a row, happen to have a lot of a certain card, it
doesn't make me think I'm more or less likely to see it with the next
guy. I don't think, on that level, metagames can be read or
predicted.

What I do think can be done is to say "Hhmm, Imbued are new/hot, I
think I'll put some Entrancement in my deck in place of a few Enchant
Kindreds." Or other stuff along those lines.

But that's just my opinion, and not really here or there. What I do
think is a good counter-argument is this: bleed is a super-common
strategy, and bounce is a super-common defense. The ubiquity of
bounce clearly hasn't made bleed a less popular strategy. Ergo,
bounce does not deter bleed.

> In my group, as mentioned in previous posts, we had a player with a
> really terrifying all-combat CEL POT Brujah rush deck. If his deck
> did more different things, then yes, combat defense would be
> appropriate. However, that's just not the case. He has so much
> combat, so many Psyches and so many Immortal Grapples, so many
> Sideslips and Blurs that you can just absolutely forget about trying
> to out-combat him at all.

You build a lot of the rest of your argument based on this idea of
unstoppable combat, leading to the conclusion that one shouldn't even
try to defend against it, and certainly not if we let combat get any
better. I disagree with this. Combat on combat is very risky stuff,
and there is no trump. He's playing 50 POT/CEL cards? Super. I'm
playing ANI/FOR, or QUI/CEL, or any number of other combat strategies
that totally tear it apart. It just seems unstoppable because your 12
or so defensive combat cards are insufficient, just like 12 bounce
won't really stop Malk94. It's just a question of numbers. I also
believe that as you slide your deck more towards unstoppable combat,
you slide it in the opposite direction with respect to actually
gaining VP's, both by ousting and by not being ousted yourself. This
is why I've always been obsessed with finding the tightest, most
minimal combat packages I can put together.

> I find the game described in the above paragraph to be very non-
> interactive.

I find it predicated upon a logical fallacy.

> All outcomes of all combats are already determined once
> deck construction is complete, and often this also means that the
> outcome of the game is already determined once seating has been
> finalized.

I have a couple of thumb-rules for Jyhad. #3 is "You are not
psychic." You don't "know" the outcome, unless the terms of
interaction on one side of the equation are zero. All you've done in
that case is create a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Or heck, maybe you are an uber-genius braniac. Plenty of people seem
to claim they can "know" the future game states on a table, but my
experience doesn't bear this out.

> What? Why would you think that I didn't use any other intercept
> cards? Just to make things clear for the rest of this, here are the
> general defenses that deck had (not the whole decklist):

OK, I didn't factor in the whole decklist, and was just going by what
you'd posted up-thread. I agree that your deck is a very flexible,
toolboxy deck that uses its Auspex to block, not just flick. But a
lot of decks are X wakes, Y bounce, and full steam ahead. Lots of
decks.

> Nah, one of the things that makes V:TES a good game is that players
> interact via card play quite a bit. If combat gets good enough to
> where you need 30-40 combat cards in order to survive until your first
> action, I really doubt it'll be very interactive at all.

Nobody is proposing that. I disagree that it would follow as a
consequence if there were merely a few more cards like Fame floating
about, since decks still need to oust and not be ousted, and it would
still be far less reliable than attacking primary resources. You need
your get into combat actions, you need some form of defense, probably
some vote defense, etc etc. I mean, we're not talking just about
weenie decks here, right?

> See, bleeding defaults to your prey, so that you can't just pool your
> resources with another player to bleed a guy out directly. But Bum's
> Rush doesn't have that default.

Right. There is no default Bum's Rush. It's more card intensive to
oust with rushing, on top of combat being more card intensive in and
of itself. These things naturally limit just how focused the deck can
get.

> And if you think two combat decks
> sitting next to each other is a bad thing, cause they'll both lose the
> game, then imagine three sitting in a row. Or all five players
> playing combat, and the one who has the trumpiest combat wins, or
> worse, the one who gets in the most combats loses. Sorry, not
> interested.

OK, I've played at plenty of tables that were fighty as hell. It's
completely unpredictable who will win, and a lot of fun. Cards flying
everywhere, and nobody knows who will be still standing when the dust
settles. Which sounds exactly like the kind of game you like. I
really think you just see your problem when a combat deck rubs up
against a deck that is only minimally prepared for combat, or not
prepared at all. Which is a strategic choice that is mostly sound,
but still not a problem with the game.

>Combat functions well right now, and just needs some more
> powerful cards. It does NOT need to be transformed into a victory
> condition.

You already conceded that combat as a victory condition was coequal
with bleed and vote, by designer intent. How can you reconcile these
two statements?

> I've played against your Fatima multirush deck a couple times, and
> it's only a lot of combat _compared to what you would expect to see_.
> It is not very much combat at all, compared to some of the crap I've
> been expected to hang on through.

I just meant "brings a lot of combat decks to tournies," not how many
red cards are in this or that deck. Fatima is tight, and tends to
lose against other decks with 50 combat cards, but those aren't the
kind of decks I'm aiming to take out, because they are very rare.

> And I'll "sort-of" concede a point right now: If rush combat IS
> given, let's say, a non-unique Fame or something, and it can oust
> players, and the BEST WAY TO DO THAT just so happens to be in a way
> where a moderate amount of combat defense can handle it, then I'm not
> opposed. I'm not in favor, mind you, but I don't think it would hurt
> the game all that much.
>
> But why would players rush with 40 combat cards, when they could rush
> with 70? I mean, if it can oust your prey now, that is?

Because that leaves 20 cards to handle every other aspect the game can
throw at you, which is likely to be a losing strategy (again, maybe
not with weenies, but I'm all in favor of doing things in a non-weenie-
enhancing way).

> Again, I don't think it would make players put in 10 more combat
> defense cards. I think it would make some players include more combat
> defense cards, until the point where the deck can't support itself
> anymore, at which point they'll just say, "screw it, if I sit next to
> rush combat, I'm dead anyway" and just play with no combat cards
> instead. And then the game is less interactive, instead of more.

Whether a deck can support itself or not is only a sensible question
when placed into the context of a particular environment. If an
environment got more fighty (but not absurdly so), then a deck that
had 10 more Flashes, and 5 less dominate bleed cards and 5 less
obfuscate stealth cards, would arguably be just as "fit."

> Yeah, but once again, where the hell are your Confusion of the Eye or
> Delaying Tactics? DI is only general defense, but I think the other
> two belong in most decks.

They are hard to fit in there, because combat is so card-intensive.
They definitely don't fit in your 70 combat card straw man.

> My point here is, you can react to the vote (which is one card) with
> another one card, and that's fine. You can't do that with combat,
> unless you know you're older than them and have Dominate, but I think
> that's really limited use. I certainly won't claim that most decks
> which fear rush would benefit from Obedience, since they're not all

an awful lot into what the OP said that wasn't necessarily there. You
seem to be assuming an awful lot about what was meant by this sentence:

able to oust folks without ever bleeding them, and going from there. I

might think so). And I think this is probably the crux in the
disagreement here--you are arguing about one thing that I suspect you
imagine that the OP was saying, and I'm not actually thinking he was
saying what you think he was saying. So we are just talking past each
other.

very prepared for combat and beating the hell out of their guy. I
still see no problem, whether the rushing player gets a GW or 0 vps.

and added Legal Manipulations & Aire of Elation.
Bob used to play an all-combat deck, learned the 0vp lesson, and added

age for a player" sort of thing. It's a good thing.

against this process.

think it's better that it not become one, unless you want all-rush

"Me" says all-combat rush is bad for the game, cause it stops other
players from playing.
"Not-me" says PTO is an effect that could also stop players from
playing.

DT, or DI to prevent PTO (which you'll note is a far smaller # of

deck.)

version of another's argument which is weaker than their actual
position, defeats the weaker position, and claims victory over the
actual position. As I was constructing my own argument using the 70-
combat-card deck, rather than trying to characterize your position as
being of it in some way, it was clearly not a straw man.

No, I don't think printing another Fame effect, or three, or ten,
would lead to 70 card combat decks (i.e. "unbeatable combat"). Combat
in the 30 - 50 range already kills minions just fine. Not all combat
disciplines are created equal, but it's clearly possible to build a
table's worth of smashing with at least a few disciplines in that
range. So, merely by taking the pool damage up from 3 for fame to,
say, 6 for Fame + foo, you aren't really incentivizing a deck full of
red cards. I think you also wouldn't see combat in the 70 range
because you still have to get a lot of other things done in a game
besides rush rush rush (again, we aren't talking about speedy weenie
rush decks here). Simply upping your rate of pool damage to your
prey, again, doesn't change that. I'd also note that it's already
possible to generate open-ended non-bleed damage from Anarch Revolt
and rushing your prey's anarchs (or blocking attempts to go anarch).
The sky hasn't fallen yet.

The other thing I wanted to clear up is any mistaken notion that I
think combat should oust as well as bleed or vote. Clearly it
shouldn't. It should always be the weakest of the three, because
you're also getting the direct benefit of minion control along with
it. In fact, you may note I am not one of the people who has weighed
in saying "Yeah, give us another damage source." If rush combat needs
anything, it's a *pool gain source*, to keep from having to vaporize
backstream so much, which tilts a table all to hell and back, but for
which many times there's just no alternative.

provides the pool padding to enable more sustained pressure forward

actually.

understand it, is that rush combat has been, historically, a pretty
marginal strategy. A strategy was was becoming less marginal until
the Imbued showed up and tipped the balance back to 'too marginal to
work reliably'.

winning to an X-N% chance of winning, where N is enough to go from

than the 'no fair playing the paper to my rock' argument.

Except that it's different in significant ways from stealth. Stealth
is relatively atomic. I play one, you play some intercept, maybe I
play another one. Combat involves, on average, a much longer chain of
cards. More importantly, it involves an escalating chain of
dependencies, where I play *this* which allows me to play *that* and
if all goes right then I get to play this *other* one. Those are
significant card flow barriers that something as simple and direct as
stealth doesn't have. Combat can't be "the other white meat" to

I was reminded again yesterday why the Imbued are so resilient against
combat decks.

It was a four-player table, I was playing my new Assamite Black-
handers and bleeding a new player who I donated my weenie-animalism
rush deck to (cos it's quite a simple, but effective strategy -
carrion crows, aid from bats, rinse-repeat). He, unfortunately, was
bleeding an Imbued gehenna heavy deck, who was bleeding a Setite S&B
temptation deck, who was bleeding me.

Yes, the Imbued did not win. The game, however, still really, really
sucked for the weenie animalism, who stood 0 chance against the
Imbued, although it would've (and did) repeatedly cream just about any
body else who got into combat with it (maybe not in each and every
combat, but over the long haul). The imbued which it did manage to
knock down did the yo-yo dance and popped out in a turn, as the imbued
player was smart enough not to waste convictions through combat.
Things got worse when a piece or two of equipment hit the table (a .44
magnum on one and a crusader sword on Jack (manuever on first round).
Events made things far worse (Thirst, Restricted Vitae, Unmasking, Dr.
Marisa Fletcher, Nightmare-upon-Nightmares, Slow Withering - in that
order).

It quickly became a war of attrition between the imbued and the
weenies, with the imbued winning by a landslide, because each torped
vampire struggled to get back into action, but each imbued (with
Jennie on the table) popped right back out in their turn - even
without Edge Explosion out and about (although there were 2 minions
with Inspire). The weenies tried to block the actions of the imbued
(with Cat's and Raven Spies), but often with little success, as the
minions with Raven Spies often collected a memories of mortality for
their trouble (sorry, no block for you).

It was just too difficult for the weenie animalism to burn the imbued
in the incapacitated region (in fact, it never managed to burn a
single one). It would often dunk another imbued/2 who blocked, but
they usually got dunked in the process as well.

It made me come to the realisation that there is no basic rule to
allow vampires to burn imbued in combat outright, unlike vampires who
can be burnt by aggravated damage. Yes, there are a few cards that
allow one to burn the imbued in combat, but these are (a) very few and
(b) very limited, i.e. Obtenebrate, Thaum, etc. are relatively rare
disciplines. This is also another aspect of the imbued that is really
powerful.

I made the glib comment then that they should introduce lethal damage
into the game (like in the role-playing game) - you know, make weapons
all deal lethal damage (by the rule-book) and if the imbued are hit
below 0-life (like agg's x+1) with a weapon, they burn out-right. It
would, at least, give combat a decent out against the Imbued that is
also useful against other vamps. I'd certainly put in a few magnum
into the weenie animalism if that was the case.

Still, I stand by my statement that a big issue for combat decks is
that it's just the imbued are too difficult to burn, and too easy to
bring back out via the yo-yo dance. There are so many ways that they
can change this to make it more reasonable, such as:

Imbued in incapacitated region don't recover conviction, but any other
imbued can burn the conviction to 'rescue' them.
Imbued require an action to recover from incapacitated.
Jennie's text only works while she is ready and applies to only 1
Imbued a turn
Imbued have the option to gain a conviction or burn conviction to
recover from incapacitated.
Imbued are tapped when they recover from incapacitated
Imbued lose all conviction and/or powers when they enter the
incapacitated region.

Those are just some ideas off the top of my head. Again, yes, I know
the imbued didn't win this game with a rush predator, but I've seen
that deck win before with a rush-predator, and it only lost because
it's prey was an uber-s&b deck who ousted everyone a turn/2 after the
Imbued had nullified it's predator and had just begun to go forward.

I have no opinion on whether the imbued are "too powerful". However,
I do feel that the above feature of the game is thematically wrong.
The imbued are (allegedly) "mortal". I have no objection to their
being tough, versatile and resilient, and well qualified to kick
monster butt, but "mortals" (of all people) should not be *immune* to
death, when facing effects that *thematically* speaking, should have
at least the potential to kill a mortal. There should be at least
*some* possibility of their being machine-gunned to death, or
decapitated with a bastard sword, or burned to a cinder with walk of
flame, of skewered in the vitals with a thrown gate, or simply ripped
apart by the nasty sharp claws and teeth of some monster with
supernatural strength.

The other day I was playing a deck that had put a hell hound in play
(yes -- I actually play that card sometimes). The hell hound was
annoying my predator by persistently blocking his weaker minions, so
he decided he'd had enough an decided to put an end to him. He rushed
him and played some effect that ought to have put an end to the poor
doggy. I whiped the satisfied smile off his face by playing "Left for
Dead".

That was unexpected. That was what made it fun. The imbued should
be more like that -- reasonably likely to survive in a well designed
deck that gives appropriate combat support cards. But when your
opponent knows, before he even enters combat with you, that you cannot
die -- knows that even after he slices you to bits with his bastard
sword, while his two ghoul retainers riddle you with bullets from
their assault rifles, he still must send someone on a special mission
to cut off your head, put a stake through your heart, burn the remains
to ashes, and bury you at a crossroads -- it takes all the fun out of
it -- besides making the imbued seem more monstrous and abnormal than
the vampires.

> I made the glib comment then that they should introduce lethal damage
> into the game (like in the role-playing game) - you know, make weapons
> all deal lethal damage (by the rule-book) and if the imbued are hit
> below 0-life (like agg's x+1) with a weapon, they burn out-right.

Aggravated damage, currently, is a vampire specific concept. Sunlight
and bright light do aggravated damage. I think it best that mortals
be different from vampires in that they are no more vulnerable to ag
damage than normal damage.

Nor do I see why weapon damage and other kinds of damage (like hand
damage) should be treated differently. Thematically, if a minion is
not powerful enough to inflict lethal damage with his hands, he cannot
hurt his enemies at all. Hence, there are plenty of mortals who
inflict zero hand damage -- they need a weapon or a lucky blow to hurt
their enemies, and many mortal allies have but one life point to
lose. The reason most vampires have 1 hand damage is because they
are supernatural monsters capable of killing with their hands. Any
mortal with 1 hand damages is unusually tough.

One could experiment with the simple rule "x+1 damage kills an
imbued". If that makes them too vulnerable, one could try "x+2 damage
kills an imbued," or introduce a rule permitting the burning of
convictions to heal damage that would otherwise burn the minion.

> It
> would, at least, give combat a decent out against the Imbued that is
> also useful against other vamps. I'd certainly put in a few magnum
> into the weenie animalism if that was the case.

Well, I agree that imbued should not be immune to a .44 magnum. But
neither do I see any thematic reason why their bodies should be immune
to being completely devoured by a swarm of carrion crows. Logically,
if you drop unconscious while being pecked to death by "carrion crows"
-- that should be curtains for you. The issue should be the amount of
damage sustained -- not the source of the damage.

> Still, I stand by my statement that a big issue for combat decks is
> that it's just the imbued are too difficult to burn, and too easy to
> bring back out via the yo-yo dance. There are so many ways that they
> can change this to make it more reasonable, such as:
>
> Imbued in incapacitated region don't recover conviction, but any other

> Imbued require an action to recover from incapacitated.
> Jennie's text only works while she is ready and applies to only 1

> recover from incapacitated.
> Imbued are tapped when they recover from incapacitated
> Imbued lose all conviction and/or powers when they enter the
> incapacitated region.

I don't think much of any of these. I think you were on the right
track with your first idea. I have no problem (thematically) with the
idea that if an imbued somehow survives combat, his vampire enemies
will have trouble interfering with his recovery. After all, the
imbued can operate in daylight, and vampires cannot.

> > flame, of skewered in the vitals with a thrown gate, or simply ripped
> > apart by the nasty sharp claws and teeth of some monster with
> > supernatural strength.
>
> Possibly, but changing each individual card to include 'lethal' damage
> would require to much of a rewriting.

Surely. I didn't anyone was suggesting such a thing.

> Including a line in the rule-
> book that states 'If an Imbued is wounded, and a weapon deals an
> additional point of damage to that Imbued, the Imbued burns instead of
> being sent to the incapacitated region" is a much shorter, succient
> solution that is far more manageable - and makes sense thematically.
> It has both mechanics and thematics on it's side.

I don't agree that it makes sense thematically, because I believe your
weapons-only distinction between lethal and non-lethal damage makes no
sense thematically.

All damage is lethal, because (setting aside the imbued) all damage
can kill a typical mortal ally. In many cases, and for most mortal
allies, a single point of damage will suffice. If a mortal ally has
more than a single life, it means he is unusually tough.

Every time a vampire burns blood to heal a point of damage, he uses
the mystical properties of blood to magically heal damage that would
kill a typical mortal.

Igo's hand damage can kill an arms dealer, or whipe out an entire pack
of gypsies. With a press or a lucky blow, Igo can whipe out a loyal
street gang. From the perspective of ordinary mortals, Igo is a
deadly supernatural monster. It is only from the perspective of more
powerful vampires that he is a wimp.

Every horror movie about werewolves I have ever seen tells me that
werewolves do not need weapons to kill mortals. Your rule implies
that a werewolf's claws and teeth are somehow not "lethal"..

> I didn't suggest the imbued that the imbued should suffer from agg - I
> just suggested they should have a 'lethal' damage equivalent that
> works with weapons instead of aggravated damage.

Right. And the weapons-only part of your proposal makes no sense to
me.

> > Nor do I see why weapon damage and other kinds of damage (like hand
> > damage) should be treated differently. Thematically, if a minion is
> > not powerful enough to inflict lethal damage with his hands, he cannot
> > hurt his enemies at all.
>
> Most roleplaying games see a difference between lethal damage and non-
> lethal damage. You can hurt someone without killing them.

Obviously, this is not that game. Any damage that cannot kill an
ordinary mortal is ignored for game purposes. Any ally that cannot
kill an ordinary mortal without benefit of a "lucky blow" has zero
hand damage.

> > Hence, there are plenty of mortals who
> > inflict zero hand damage -- they need a weapon or a lucky blow to hurt
> > their enemies, and many mortal allies have but one life point to
> > lose.
>
> Or they have 0 hand damage cos they can't throw a punch.

That makes no sense thematically. Usually, for a mortal, 0 strength
means that they do not ordinarily carry lethal hand weapons. Carlton
Van Wyck, a capable vampire hunter, is presumably capable of throwing
a punch; but normally carries handgun rather than a hand weapon --
hence he has inherent 1R damage and 0 strength. Same logic applies to
Survivalist and Wendell Delburton. A Courier is presumably fit and
healthy, but has 0 strength, because he does not normally carry lethal
weapons on his bike. Street Gangs and Arms Dealers have 1 strength,
because they ordinarily carry lethal weapons.

> > The reason most vampires have 1 hand damage is because they
> > are supernatural monsters capable of killing with their hands. Any
> > mortal with 1 hand damages is unusually tough.
>
> And yet the roleplaying game (and all versions of it, might I add) all
> distinguish between normal damage and lethal damage - and often the
> distinction is found in the weapons of the game.

Obviously, this rule has not been incorporated into the card game.

> Sure there would be
> some strange cases where the weapon would be technically non-lethal,
> such as brass knuckles, but this would be a small minority over a very
> large majority (especially of played) weapons that are lethal.

Thematically, all damage is lethal. One point of damage kills an
ordinary mortal.

> > One could experiment with the simple rule "x+1 damage kills an
> > imbued". If that makes them too vulnerable, one could try "x+2 damage
> > kills an imbued," or introduce a rule permitting the burning of
> > convictions to heal damage that would otherwise burn the minion.
>
> Then I fear it would be far too easy to burn an imbued, and they would
> be come far too vulnerable to decent combat. Or alternatively if your X
> + gets too high, then it would become far too cornercase.

In which case, perhaps they need appropriate combat defense cards.
Thematically, I see no other solution.,

> > > It
> > > would, at least, give combat a decent out against the Imbued that is
> > > also useful against other vamps. I'd certainly put in a few magnum
> > > into the weenie animalism if that was the case.
>
> > Well, I agree that imbued should not be immune to a .44 magnum. But
> > neither do I see any thematic reason why their bodies should be immune
> > to being completely devoured by a swarm of carrion crows. Logically,
> > if you drop unconscious while being pecked to death by "carrion crows"
> > -- that should be curtains for you. The issue should be the amount of
> > damage sustained -- not the source of the damage.
>
> Again, my solution is both thematically appropriate and thematically
> strong.

Thematically is precisely how your solution is inappropriate.

> Your solutions may make thematic sense, but really fall short
> on the mechanics, being either far too difficult to implement, or
> changing things far too dramatically, to the point where Imbued become
> ultra-weak.

Well, I'll have to try it out.

> Especially since you could argue your case for what
> happens to vampires after they are torporized. Why can't the gangrel
> stick around an extra round after you've been knocked out to tear you
> completely apart with his claws?

Seems to me that this is an entirely separate thematic "problem".
Perhaps it would be contrary to his nature. His temptation would be
to commit diablerie. Perhaps resisting that temptation means walking
away and leaving the body where it lies.

Moreover, Gangrel *can* kill in combat. A lucky blow with wolf claws,
to a vampire with no blood, does the trick. Who are you to say this
does not represent multiple blows. I'm sure when Igo the Hungry
whipes out an entire loyal street gang with a "lucky blow", we are
supposed to imagine this actually represents multiple blows.

> Because it would break the mechanics
> of the game.

And yet Gangrel *do* tear apart their opponents during combat (burn
them in combat) and the mechanics of the game are not broken.

> > > Imbued in incapacitated region don't recover conviction, but any other
> > > imbued can burn the conviction to 'rescue' them.
> > > Imbued require an action to recover from incapacitated.
> > > Jennie's text only works while she is ready and applies to only 1
> > > Imbued a turn
> > > Imbued have the option to gain a conviction or burn conviction to
> > > recover from incapacitated.
> > > Imbued are tapped when they recover from incapacitated
> > > Imbued lose all conviction and/or powers when they enter the
> > > incapacitated region.
>
> > I don't think much of any of these.> I think you were on the right
> > track with your first idea. I have no problem (thematically) with the
> > idea that if an imbued somehow survives combat, his vampire enemies
> > will have trouble interfering with his recovery. After all, the
> > imbued can operate in daylight, and vampires cannot.
>
> Of all the options I've listed only 1 of them actually would
> potentially have any vampire interference. All the rest (5) are purely
> looking at the imbued

Almost all of them look at their ability to recover once
incapacitated. I just don't see that as a thematic problem.

even if it's not strictly. But as 90% of the weapons in the card game
would be considered as dealing lethal damage in the roleplaying game,
I would be willing to live with it thematically.

>

interpretation. Nowhere has this been made explicit, and thus talking
about it 'thematically' is the theme according to you. At least my
thematical distinction is based on the roleplaying game, and not
personal interpretation of the way the VTES world is.

>

it's own right, but that sufficient weapons are lethal, enough to
warrant that they all would deal lethal (killing) damage to the
imbued. They may release other cards later that deal lethal damage as
well, but I wouldn't suggest rewriting all the old cards.

>
> Obviously, this is not that game.

game. The roleplaying game has a distinction between lethal and non-
lethal damage that lethal damage kills mortals far more readily than
non-lethal damage does. Taking into account that the Imbued are more
combat resilient than normal mortals, I'd expect them to be more
resilient to normal methods of damage, but still not be as resilient
to lethal damage as a vampire is.

And in the roleplaying game, your 'hand damage' is never lethal, even
with martial arts training - although it may still kill mortals.

> Any damage that cannot kill an
> ordinary mortal is ignored for game purposes. Any ally that cannot
> kill an ordinary mortal without benefit of a "lucky blow" has zero
> hand damage.

Well, all the Vampire roleplaying games have this distinction. If

probably have had lethal damage included.

>
> > Or they have 0 hand damage cos they can't throw a punch.

> That makes no sense thematically. Usually, for a mortal, 0 strength

I disagree with this reasoning. I'd say they have the 1 strength
because they know how to fight, fit and healthy means extra life, but

> > > mortal with 1 hand damages is unusually tough.

> > And yet the roleplaying game (and all versions of it, might I add) all

> Obviously, this rule has not been incorporated into the card game.

Because there was no reason to before hand - all allies burnt when
they hit 0.

> > Sure there would be
> > some strange cases where the weapon would be technically non-lethal,
> > such as brass knuckles, but this would be a small minority over a very
> > large majority (especially of played) weapons that are lethal.
>
> Thematically, all damage is lethal. One point of damage kills an
> ordinary mortal.

Burn =/= kill. When I use the word 'lethal' I don't mean it in the
dictionary sense of the word, I mean it in the role-playing game sense
of the word - which is how I brought it up - by saying that they have
no 'lethal' damage equivalent from the roleplaying game as they have
an 'aggravated' damage equivalent. I think you may be talking about
lethal damage in the dictionary sense.

> > > damage sustained -- not the source of the damage.
>
> > Again, my solution is both thematically appropriate and thematically
> > strong.
>
> Thematically is precisely how your solution is inappropriate.

We'll have to agree to disagree. My understanding of the card game and
how it relates to the roleplaying game, says that it is possible to
interpret damage from weapons in that way. Some damage is just more
likely to kill you than it is to maim you.

>
> > Your solutions may make thematic sense, but really fall short
> > on the mechanics, being either far too difficult to implement, or
> > changing things far too dramatically, to the point where Imbued become
> > ultra-weak.
>
> Well, I'll have to try it out.

Please do, and then let me know how the mechanics work out.

> > Especially since you could argue your case for what

> > stick around an extra round after you've been knocked out to tear you
> > completely apart with his claws?

> to commit diablerie. Perhaps resisting that temptation means walking
> away and leaving the body where it lies.

And how would this relate to leaving a mortal ally lying in
incapacitated. Would the vampire have the same problems? Would they
just let the mortals be taken away by the ambulance? Not such a huge
thematic difference there now, is there?

>
> Moreover, Gangrel *can* kill in combat. A lucky blow with wolf claws,
> to a vampire with no blood, does the trick. Who are you to say this
> does not represent multiple blows. I'm sure when Igo the Hungry
> whipes out an entire loyal street gang with a "lucky blow", we are
> supposed to imagine this actually represents multiple blows.

Or that it represents a lucky blow to the leader that scares the shit
out of all the others and cause them to flee. Again - it's up to
interpretation. Thematics should only carry an argument so far. As
long as it is not thematically completely inappropriate, implementing
any rule will be fine so long as the mechanics are sound.

> > Because it would break the mechanics
> > of the game.
>
> And yet Gangrel *do* tear apart their opponents during combat (burn
> them in combat) and the mechanics of the game are not broken.
>

Not even close to often enough to consider it broken.

>
> > Of all the options I've listed only 1 of them actually would
> > potentially have any vampire interference. All the rest (5) are purely
> > looking at the imbued
>
> Almost all of them look at their ability to recover once
> incapacitated. I just don't see that as a thematic problem.

Yes, but these are a mechanical problem in the game that can be
explained via thematics. For example, an imbued that gets the snot
kicked out of him, might lose some of his faith in the cause (i.e.
lose all their conviction), or imbued don't get out of hospital ready
to go running around doing the errands of a methuselah immediately,
they might need to 'tap' in order to get back home or to their base of
operations or whatever.

You are getting far too hung up on thematics. I say fixing the
mechanics comes first, then find a way to make it thematically fit in
- and if that's not possible, then find another solution.

The weapon distinction is a mechanical solution - it's good for weapon
combat decks, which aren't very popular or common especially when
compared with the number of vote decks, or s&b decks. In fact, they
are probably far less common than Imbued decks are in the tournament
scene. Helping out combat with an obvious weakness seems very
mechanically sound to me.

Then the thematics can be explained away by the same reasoning they
use in the roleplaying game - i.e. it is far easier to kill mortals
with weapons than your bare fists, and it's far more difficult for a
mortal to sustain a blow with a bastard sword than it is to sustain
the same level of damage from a fist (e.g. a vampire throwing a
haymaker).

Sure, some other cards could have done 'lethal' damage, but then some
other cards should already affect the imbued that don't - such as
decapitate and disarm. At this point in the game, it would be far too
difficult to change that, but the weapon mechanic is very easy to
change in comparison.

>
> > On Oct 30, 8:46 pm, nyst...@cs.com wrote:
> > > All damage is lethal, because (setting aside the imbued) all damage
> > > can kill a typical mortal ally. In many cases, and for most mortal
> > > allies, a single point of damage will suffice. If a mortal ally has
> > > more than a single life, it means he is unusually tough.
>
> > > Every time a vampire burns blood to heal a point of damage, he uses
> > > the mystical properties of blood to magically heal damage that would
> > > kill a typical mortal.
>
> > No, he uses a blood to heal damage that would typically 'wound' them.
>
> Where's the contradiction? You "wound" a vampire when you shove a
> stake through his heart. What do you think that does to a typical
> mortal?

My point is that you are adding in your own extra bit - that being
that damage that would 'wound' a vampire is the same thing as damage
that would kill a typical mortal. While is may be in some
circumstances, it won't be in most. (It's the: "All dogs have four
legs. All dogs are animals. Hence all animals are dogs." argument.)
Just because typical mortals can be killed with one point of damage in
the card game, and all imbued are mortal, does not mean that they
should be equally easy to kill (with a single point of damage). Imbued
are supernatural mortals.

>
> > Saying that this damage would kill a typical mortal is up for
> > interpretation.
>
> No. This is a cold hard fact. No interpretation required. Not
> counting imbued, 31 retainer or ally cards, representing single
> mortals, have been printed. 22 of them have 1 life, 7 have 2 life,
> and 2 have 3 life. (Of those 7 cards representing multiple mortals, 1
> has 1 life, 4 have 2 life, and 2 have 3 life).

Again, that is up for interpretation - a typical mortal need not die
in order to no longer be in your ready region. They could just as
easily have been beat up, and left your cause for it, but still be
perfectly alive.

> > Nowhere has this been made explicit, and thus talking
> > about it 'thematically' is the theme according to you.
>
> Simple observation.

No. Simple thumb sucking interpretation of a mechanic that has never
been made explicit thematically.

> > At least my
> > thematical distinction is based on the roleplaying game, and not
> > personal interpretation of the way the VTES world is.
>
> At least my observations are based on the right game.

No. They're based on your interpreted observations of the game, and
your specific way of visualising what is happening. There are other
ways of interpreting it which is perfectly reasonable.

> > As I said, I'm not saying that other damage would not be lethal in
> > it's own right, but that sufficient weapons are lethal, enough to
> > warrant that they all would deal lethal (killing) damage to the
> > imbued. They may release other cards later that deal lethal damage as
> > well, but I wouldn't suggest rewriting all the old cards.
>
> Anything capable of inflicting a single point of damage is lethal.
> One damage snuffs out one "life".

One life in the mechanics sense, but not necessarily one life in the
dictionary sense.

>
> > > > Most roleplaying games see a difference between lethal damage and non-
> > > > lethal damage. You can hurt someone without killing them.
>
> > > Obviously, this is not that game.
>
> > Actually, it is that game - this game is based on the roleplaying
> > game.
>
> Different game. Different mechanics. Similar thematics.

Yes, and that is why I'm looking at the thematics of the RPG to
interpret thematically a change to the rules (i.e. mechanics) of the
card game. I am not saying that because it is in the RPG, it should be
in the CCG. I'm saying the CCG needs a mechanic to make Imbued able to
burn via combat, looking at the RPG for inspiration and thematical
guidance, and introducing a mechanic into the CCG which is
thematically justified by the RPG. It's really, really tough to base
any thematic discussion on anything but the RPG, as it is completely
open to interpretation otherwise.

>
> > The roleplaying game has a distinction between lethal and non-
> > lethal damage that lethal damage kills mortals far more readily than
> > non-lethal damage does.
>
> Different mechanics. A card game cannot be expected to have mechanics
> as intricate as an RPG.

I'm not asking the CCG to have the same mechanics as the RPG. I'm
saying the CCG needs a mechanic to make the Imbued able to burn in
combat. I'm offering a suggestion for that mechanic. And then I'm
saying that it fits in thematically as seen in the RPG.

> In the card game, the distinction between
> lethal and non-lethal is represented by "at least 1 damage" as
> distinct from "0 damage".

Again, that's your interpretation. I would say that there is an
equally strong reason to believe that the distinction between lethal
and non-lethal damage is not at all made in the CCG, as there was
never a need for it prior to the Imbued. Allies burnt when they hit 0
life, and vampires treat 'lethal' damage in the same way they treat
'non-lethal' damage.

>
> > Taking into account that the Imbued are more
> > combat resilient than normal mortals, I'd expect them to be more
> > resilient to normal methods of damage, but still not be as resilient
> > to lethal damage as a vampire is.
>
