> burn in combat than vampires. I just don't see why such a solution
> should involve a "lethal damage" rule.

Because it's a simple mechanic that can be thematically justified and
has the right level of balance. I haven't heard any other suggestion
that has all three of these things yet. Mostly they seem unbalanced
(too powerful or too weak).

>
> > And in the roleplaying game, your 'hand damage' is never lethal, even
> > with martial arts training - although it may still kill mortals.
>
> I don't see how the mechanics of the RPG are relevant. Thematics?
> Yes. Mechanics? No.

Again, I'm suggesting a mechanic into the CCG and using the RPG to
thematically justify it. The only thing taken from the mechanics of
the RPG is a distinction between lethal and non-lethal damage (i.e.
the actual terminology) and the fact that weapons in the RPG typically
do lethal damage whereas fists do not. The actual mechanics of this in
the RPG are very, very different to what I'm suggesting here (as it
deals mostly with how mortals & vamps soak/prevent lethal damage -
which is not the mechanic I'm introducing here).

> > Well, all the Vampire roleplaying games have this distinction. If
> > there were mortal crypt cards to begin with in the card game, it would
> > probably have had lethal damage included.
>
> The original card game did include many mortals -- and lethal damage
> (simply "damage") was included. One damage burns one "life". I don't
> see how it is relevant that they were not crypt cards.

It is relevant in the sense that those mortals don't have an
incapacitated region. When they become 'incapacitated' they leave your
cause (are burnt) - this may or may not be due to actual death -
especially if you think about playing the same unique mortal (e.g.
Moise Kasavubu gets burnt, then you bring out another Moise - it's
kinda saying the first one didn't actually die, it just left your
cause for a while.)

> You also forget that in the original game, most melee weapons were
> (and still are) very large. A bastard sword inflicted +1 damage.
> Small knives and switchblades have never been included in the game.
> They are too small and insignificant to count for damage purposes, and
> maybe are too small (thematically) to be affected by immortal
> grapple.

Yes, which is exactly why I say it's difficult to work with thematics
first, and mechanics second. Make the mechanic first, then justify it
via thematics. If it can't be justified, toss it, and start again.

> It is all relative. A courrier is no match for an entire street gang,
> or even an entire pack of gypsies. But he can still take out an
> eccentric billionaire with a lucky blow.

My point exactly. It's relative - i.e. it's open to interpretation.
You have been using your interpretation of the thematics of the CCG to
discredit my suggestion - which is a relative argument. My
interpretation is just as feasible as yours, except that my 'lethal
weapon' mechanic actually has merit as far as mechanics and game
balance is concerned - an issue that you have not addressed.

Putting thematics aside (which as I have said can be interpreted in
different ways), is the mechanic a balanced one? I would say very much
so.

Then: Can it be justified through thematics? I would also say so - in
that it can be easily interpreted in that way, even if it can be
equally interpreted another way. Nothing you can say will be able to
make my interpretation seem completely unreasonable, just as nothing I
can say can make your interpretation unreasonable. Both are equally
good interpretations.

> > Because there was no reason to before hand - all allies burnt when
> > they hit 0.
>
> Exactly. There is no need for a "lethal damage" rule, because all
> damage is lethal.

In the dictionary sense of the word - which is not the sense I was
using it. My lethal damage rule is just stating that some kinds of
damage (particularly those of weapons) are more lethal (i.e. more
likely to lead to death) than other kinds of damages. Being hit by a
bastard sword is far more likely to lead to death than a good haymaker
shot - which is more likely to lead to you being knocked unconscious.

> 3 damage kills a werewolf, for chrissakes. The
> thematic problem with imbued is that they are immune to ordinary (but
> perfectly lethal) damage.

Not immune, just resilient. I believe their resilience can be
reasonable dropped for weapons - and still be balanced in the game.

> > Burn =/= kill. When I use the word 'lethal' I don't mean it in the
> > dictionary sense of the word, I mean it in the role-playing game sense
> > of the word - which is how I brought it up - by saying that they have
> > no 'lethal' damage equivalent from the roleplaying game as they have
> > an 'aggravated' damage equivalent. I think you may be talking about
> > lethal damage in the dictionary sense.
>
> Of course. I am discussing thematics. Why discuss the mechanics of a
> different game?

It's not discussing the mechanics of another game. It's discussing the
thematics and terminology of another game. For example, if there was
no aggravated damage in the CCG, and I wanted to introduce the
concept, I would refer to the idea of aggravated damage as it is in
the RPG (i.e. use their terminology). Unless you also want to
discredit aggravated damage because of it's dictionary definition. I'm
only using the terminology, as explained in the RPG, in the same way
aggravated damage uses the terminology of the RPG.

I could change the term from lethal to "Fizz-whopper" damage if you
like - which would mean damage that is much more likely to kill than
severely maim a mortal. I would put a vampires fists in the NON-fizz-
whopper category, and most weapons in the fizz-whopper category, even
if you take into account things like undead strength and haymakers and
lucky blows etc.

fists and machine guns and the human body.

until their body regenerates enough to be fully active (shuffling back
into your deck until you draw the card or a copy again), and you can
entice them back into doing your dirty work (i.e. you pay pool to

scatter to the winds until a new leader is found (the gang being
brought back into play by whatever means) is certainly not a stretch
of the imagination.

must by default be killed outright. In my mind, though, Pool
represents the resources at the Metheselah has available. This could
be money, policitical clout or supernatural power, all of which is
used to Influence (i.e. buy the services of) Vampires and other
creatures of the night. Losing your last pool ends your influence in
worldly affairs, but doesn't necessarily mean that Igo found your
little hidey hole and put and end to you once and for all.

Both do. The concept of "healing", as referenced here, is applicable
only to vampires. In VTES, allies may gain or lose life, but they do
not "heal". "Healing" in VTES, refers to a vampire burning blood to
avoid torpor, and that is EXACTLY the rules mechanism that is being
discussed here.

prevent a Renegade Garou from regenerating.

Yes easily. I'll let you decide what "sufficiently high" is, but, if

If you think this is a problem, then increase the requirement so that
most potence strikes, coupled with increased strength, will not
normally burn them. What is it about "sufficiently high" that you did
not understand?

With the right combo, you can also inflict large amounts of agg
damage. If "x+2 agg damage to burn" makes vamps reasonably resilient,
then "x+4 normal damage to burn" should make an imbued reasonably
resilient. And if you don't like X+4, go to X+5.

The above assumes that your goal is to make allies just as hard to
burn as vampires. Thematically, I don't think this should be the
goal. I think it would be better if Imbued were easier to burn in
combat than vampires, but were counterbalanced in other ways (as with

card: Fake Out. If you want to counter the Fake Out, you are dealing
with a 4-card combo

nys...@cs.com writes:
>Right. This resembles the old "DPTES" position, as in, "the game
>could be called 'Dog Poo: The Eternal Struggle' and it would make no
>difference to me, as I am only interested in the wonderful game
>mechanics."

There are those of us who would play DP:TES because the game would be
fun, but who like having a decent theme when possible.

However, theme is rarely a good reason to:

- initiate change in the first place
- use a complicated system in preference to a simple one
- have specific, corner-case rules that don't generalize well to other
facets of the game (e.g. Paralyze, Close Quarters)

and that sort of thing.

Theme is great for getting inspiration, design ideas, and so on, but it
should never be an overriding concern. The card game must hang together
as a card game.

This means that even those who don't have much interest in theme may
have some desire to make sure that certain thematic aspects are ignored
or employed, where possible. As you say elsewhere, thematics are
subject to interpretation. If I'd rather have a different system in
place then, even if I don't personally care much about thematics, it may
be in my interests to suggest a meaningful interpretation to get those
people who do care considering and supporting my proposal, or to get
useful WoD-oriented names for new counters, new damage, new rules etc.

This is "normal" up to a point.

For a non-unique ally/retainer, it seems a reasonable assumption. The
new Wolf Companion I bring out is a new one. I summon up a shadow and
it really doesn't have to be the same shadow.

For unique allies/retainers, it's significantly trickier to work out
what the "normal thematic assumption" is. You can bring out Mr Winthrop
and have him murdered, then bring him out again, have him murdered
again, and bring him out yet again. No Necromancy needed to reanimate
him. No Vicissitude, fleshcrafting him back from the brink of his
organs spilling out of his body. No Chimerical illusion so it's not
actually Mr Winthrop but his brother with a spell on him. From the
game's point of view, it's just Mr Winthrop again. Normal thematic
assumption? Reports of his death *may* have been grossly exaggerated.

The same is also true of vampires, where there have long been thematic
issues with vampires who were burned or diablerized coming back without
any special effort being expended.
